subsystems.name: Skin and contact surface
subsystems.role: the deformable outer layer that touches objects and converts contact into a measurable change.

subsystems.name: Transduction layer
subsystems.role: turns mechanical deformation into an electronic signal.

subsystems.name: Readout electronics
subsystems.role: captures and digitises the raw sensor signal.

subsystems.name: Signal processing and models
subsystems.role: reconstructs contact geometry, normal and shear forces, and texture.

subsystems.name: Mechanical integration
subsystems.role: mounts the sensor on a robot finger or hand and protects it.

subsystems.name: Calibration and control interface
subsystems.role: maps sensor output to physical units and feeds it to the robot controller.

buildSteps.title: Design the elastomer skin
buildSteps.detail: Choose a silicone with the right stiffness and durability; cast it in a mould and cure. For optical sensors, add a pattern of markers or a reflective membrane on the inner face.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the sensing surface
buildSteps.detail: For capacitive arrays, deposit and pattern electrodes on a flexible substrate. For optical sensors, polish the gel to an even thickness and bond it to a transparent window.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the optical or electronic stack
buildSteps.detail: Place a small camera and LEDs beneath the gel, or connect the electrode array to readout chips. Align precisely so the field of view covers the whole contact area.

buildSteps.title: Integrate readout electronics
buildSteps.detail: Connect the sensor to a microcontroller and data interface on a flexible circuit board that fits inside a fingertip.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate with known forces
buildSteps.detail: Press the sensor with controlled weights and indenters, record the response, and fit a model that converts raw signals into force and position.

buildSteps.title: Train perception models
buildSteps.detail: Use the calibrated data to train machine learning models that estimate shear, slip and texture from the sensor output.

buildSteps.title: Package and mount
buildSteps.detail: Seal the sensor in a robust housing, attach it to a robot finger, and route cables without restricting motion.

buildSteps.title: Validate in manipulation tasks
buildSteps.detail: Test the sensor by having a robot grasp, rotate and identify objects; measure resolution, repeatability and durability.

prerequisites.why: optical tactile sensors image a deformable surface at close range, so they need small, sharp cameras.
dense sensor arrays must be wired and read out without stiff, bulky cables that limit finger motion.
raw tactile images are high-dimensional; models are needed to extract force, slip and texture in real time.
the skin must survive thousands of contacts without tearing or losing sensitivity.
a camera-based sensor produces video-rate data that must reach the controller fast enough for feedback.

pathway.milestone: lab and early commercial optical tactile sensors (such as GelSight) used in research grippers
pathway.unlocks: proven ability to measure fine contact geometry and texture.

pathway.milestone: sensors integrated into commercial robot hands for grasping and assembly
pathway.unlocks: reliable pick-and-place of delicate or unknown objects.

pathway.milestone: full-hand or arm-covering tactile skin with onboard processing
pathway.unlocks: safe physical interaction and richer manipulation.

pathway.milestone: human-level resolution and durability in a thin, cheap skin
pathway.unlocks: general-purpose dexterous robots in homes, farms and factories.
